v.q: Why is `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update` a poor way to manage a production schema?
o: It guesses the difference at start-up, never drops or renames, cannot change data and differs per environment
It is slower than any migration tool because it scans every table on each request
It only works with H2 and is ignored by PostgreSQL
It stores the schema in the application jar instead of the database
v.w: Explicit, reviewed, ordered scripts are repeatable and auditable. update only guesses a diff.

v.q: What do you gain from keeping schema changes as migrations in Git?
o: The same ordered changes reach every environment, each applied once, and reviewable in a pull request
The database no longer needs backups because the scripts can rebuild the data
Queries run faster because the optimizer reads the scripts
The application no longer needs a database connection pool
v.w: Repeatability, an audit trail and a gate in the pipeline. Data still needs backups.

v.q: Which file name is a valid Flyway versioned migration?
o: V3__add_status.sql
V3_add_status.sql
add_status_V3.sql
3-add-status.sql
v.w: V, the version, two underscores, then the description.

v.q: Which Flyway migration is re-applied whenever its content changes?
o: R__account_summary_view.sql
V1__account_summary_view.sql
U1__account_summary_view.sql
B1__account_summary_view.sql
v.w: Repeatable migrations start with R__ and run again when their checksum changes, after the versioned ones.

v.q: What is the purpose of the flyway_schema_history table?
o: It records which migrations were applied to this database, with checksums, so only the missing ones run
It stores a copy of every row that each migration changed
It holds the application's audit log of user actions
It caches the compiled SQL so migrations start faster
v.w: One row per migration: version, description, checksum, time and result.

v.q: Which tables does Liquibase create in your database?
o: DATABASECHANGELOG and DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK
LIQUIBASE_HISTORY and LIQUIBASE_USERS
SCHEMA_VERSION only
CHANGESET_LOG and MIGRATION_QUEUE
v.w: The first lists applied changesets with checksums, the second holds the lock row.

v.q: A developer edits V2__add_status.sql after it ran in production. What happens at the next deploy?
o: Validation fails on the checksum mismatch and the application does not start
Flyway silently applies the new content again
Flyway ignores the file because its version is already recorded
Flyway deletes the old row and runs the file as a new migration
v.w: The recorded checksum no longer matches. Revert the edit and add a new migration.

v.q: What is the correct fix for an edited, already applied migration?
o: Revert the edit and put the change in a new migration
Run clean so the schema is rebuilt
Delete the row from the history table and redeploy
Rename the file so the version changes
v.w: clean destroys data and is disabled by default. Editing history is exactly what the tool prevents.

v.q: Which kind of object suits a repeatable migration?
o: A view or function that is replaced as a whole
A table creation that must run only once
A column rename
A foreign key added to existing data
v.w: Repeatable migrations re-run when they change, so they must be safe to apply again.

v.q: When does a repeatable migration run relative to versioned ones?
o: After all pending versioned migrations
Before any versioned migration
Only on a fresh empty database
Only when the application runs in the dev profile
v.w: Repeatable ones always run last, in description order.

v.q: How does Liquibase identify a changeset?
o: By id, author and file path together
By the file name only
By the checksum alone
By its position in the master changelog
v.w: Moving or renaming a file changes the identity unless logicalFilePath is set.

v.q: What is the risk of renaming a changelog file that holds already applied changesets?
o: The path is part of the identity, so Liquibase may treat them as new and run them again
The history table is dropped
Nothing, the file name is not recorded
The database locks until the file is renamed back
v.w: Use logicalFilePath to keep the old identity when a file must move.

v.q: Two pods start at once and both have Flyway enabled. What prevents the same migration running twice?
o: A database lock: one instance migrates and the other waits
The load balancer sends only one pod to start
Each pod migrates a different half of the scripts
Kubernetes starts pods one at a time by default
v.w: Both tools lock the database first. A separate migration step avoids the race altogether.

v.q: Liquibase waits for a lock that nobody holds, after a crashed run. What clears it?
o: release-locks, after checking that no migration is running
clear-checksums
rollback-count 1
Dropping the DATABASECHANGELOG table
v.w: The DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK row stayed locked by the killed process.

v.q: Why do many banks run migrations as a pipeline step instead of at application start?
o: A failure stops the release before traffic moves, and the application account needs no DDL rights
Migrations are not allowed to run inside Java
Spring Boot cannot run Flyway at start-up
It makes each migration run in parallel on every pod
v.w: Also one runner, one log, and slow migrations do not fail readiness probes.

v.q: Which account should the running application use in production?
o: A least-privilege account without DDL rights, while a schema-owner account runs the migrations
The schema owner, so it can fix problems itself
The database administrator account
A shared account named after the environment
v.w: Separating the two limits what a compromised service can do.

v.q: You add Flyway to a database that already has tables. What does baselining do?
o: Records the existing schema as already at version N, so only later migrations run
Drops the tables and recreates them from the scripts
Copies the data into a new schema
Disables checksum validation permanently
v.w: Without a baseline the tool would try to create tables that already exist.

v.q: Which Liquibase commands adopt an existing database?
o: generate-changelog, then changelog-sync
update, then rollback
diff, then clean
tag, then release-locks
v.w: The first captures the schema, the second marks it as already applied.

v.q: What is the usual way to undo a bad migration in production?
o: Roll forward with a new migration
Edit the old migration and redeploy
Run clean and rebuild
Delete the history row and run it again
v.w: A fix-forward migration is tested and recorded like any other change.

v.q: Why is a rollback script not a full safety net?
o: It restores structure, but data that was dropped or overwritten is gone
It can only run on an empty database
It always locks the table forever
It is not recorded in the history table
v.w: That is why changes are made backward compatible and destructive steps come later.

v.q: Why must a migration work with the previous application version?
o: During a rolling release or a rollback the old code runs against the new schema
Flyway only supports the previous version
The old version reads the migration files at start-up
Liquibase refuses to run if the code changed
v.w: Hence expand and contract: add first, remove in a later release.

v.q: Which change is safe to ship in the same release as the code that stops using the column?
o: Adding a new nullable column
Dropping the old column
Renaming the old column
Changing the column type in place
v.w: Drop and rename must wait until no old version can return.

v.q: Which ddl-auto value fits production when Flyway owns the schema?
o: validate (or none)
update
create
create-drop
v.w: validate makes the application fail fast if the schema and entities disagree, without changing anything.

v.q: An entity gets a new field but no migration. With ddl-auto=validate, what happens?
o: The application fails at start-up with a schema-validation error
Hibernate adds the column automatically
The field is ignored silently
Flyway generates the migration at run time
v.w: That is the safety net. Add the migration, never switch to update.

v.q: A multi-statement migration fails halfway on MySQL. Why is this worse than on PostgreSQL?
o: MySQL commits DDL implicitly, so the earlier statements stay applied
MySQL cannot run SQL migrations
PostgreSQL ignores errors in migrations
MySQL deletes the history table on failure
v.w: PostgreSQL runs DDL in a transaction, so the script rolls back whole.

v.q: How do you reduce the damage of a half-applied migration?
o: One logical change per file, rehearsed on a production-sized copy
Put every change of a release into one big file
Disable the history table
Run it twice to be sure
v.w: Small files fail small and are easy to repair.

v.q: How do you add a NOT NULL constraint to a huge table without a long lock?
o: Add the column nullable, backfill in batches, then add the constraint as NOT VALID and validate it
Add it with NOT NULL and no default and let it run
Stop the application and run one UPDATE for all rows
Recreate the table from a dump during business hours
v.w: Each step holds locks briefly, and a short lock_timeout makes a blocked statement fail rather than queue.

v.q: Why set a short lock_timeout on a migration statement?
o: So it fails fast instead of queuing behind a long query and blocking everything behind it
So the statement runs faster once it has the lock
So the checksum is calculated sooner
So the history table is not written
v.w: A waiting ALTER TABLE blocks new queries on that table while it waits.

v.q: Two branches each add V5__something.sql and both merge. What happens?
o: Flyway fails with a duplicate-version error
Both run, in alphabetical order, without a message
The newer file silently replaces the older one
Flyway renumbers one of them automatically
v.w: Catch it in CI, renumber before merging, or use timestamp versions.

v.q: Which versioning style makes version clashes between branches much less likely?
o: Timestamp based versions such as V20261123_1030
Using the same number for every file
Using only repeatable migrations
Skipping descriptions in file names
v.w: Timestamps rarely collide, though they can then arrive out of order.
